name: pam-mysql bypass
tile_line: SSH in as users with no stored password. Rare module.
tldr: A rarely used login module, pam-mysql, lets anyone SSH in as an account with no stored password, typing any password. Exploit demonstrated, not published; no attacks. If you use it, install Debian's fix where available, or delete password-less rows.
summary: pam-mysql checks Linux logins against a MySQL table and gets one check backwards; with sshd's default settings that's enough for an SSH login. Debian fixed it on 19 Nov 2026; Ubuntu and Fedora haven't yet.

affected.label: pam-mysql checks your logins
affected.text: The module is in the PAM setup of a login service such as sshd, the case the researcher tested. Every released version has the bug, 0.8.x and the 1.0.0 betas. Few systems use it: Debian counts 190 installs. A file name in the output means it's in use for that service.

affected.label: The service refuses empty passwords
affected.text: That is sshd's default (`PermitEmptyPasswords no`), and it's what triggers the bug: sshd asks pam-mysql to refuse accounts with no password, and pam-mysql does the opposite. Don't switch it to `yes` as a fix; the researcher says that opens a different hole. Run as root.

affected.label: Some accounts have no password
affected.text: At least one row in the login table has no stored password. On 0.8.x (Debian, Ubuntu, Gentoo, FreeBSD) that means NULL. On the 1.0.0 betas (Fedora, Nix, Mageia, ALT) an empty string counts too, so the common `NOT NULL DEFAULT ''` column is exposed; the researcher says PostfixAdmin and Froxlor ship tables like that. Replace the table and column names with yours.
affected.cmd: SELECT username FROM users WHERE password IS NULL OR password='';

affected.label: The package isn't patched
affected.text: Fixed: Debian 13 `0.8.2-2.1+deb13u1` and Debian 12 `0.8.2-2+deb12u1`. Some news sites give `0.8.2-2.1` as fixed for Debian 13; Debian lists that version as vulnerable. Not fixed yet on 21 Nov 2026: Debian testing and unstable, Ubuntu ("needs evaluation"), Fedora and Gentoo. On Fedora the package is `pam_mysql`.

do.label: Update the package
do.text: On Debian 12 and 13, install the update from DSA-6643-1 or DLA-4919-1. The fix adds a `nullok` option, off by default, so accounts with no password are refused. Elsewhere there's no fixed package yet: upstream fixed its 1.0 code on 19 Nov 2026 but hasn't tagged a release, and its 0.8.x branch has no fix.

do.label: No update yet? Fill the gaps
do.text: Stop storing accounts with no password in any table used for logins: delete those rows, then make the password column `NOT NULL` with no empty-string default. That's the researcher's fix for unpatched systems. Don't set `PermitEmptyPasswords yes`.

do.label: Check past logins
do.text: sshd logs a bypass exactly like a normal login ("Accepted password for"). Any password login by an account that had no stored password at the time was a bypass. The table as it is now may not show what it held then; a backup or the binary log does. pam-mysql's own log table is off by default, and when on it spells failures `AUTHENTICATION FALURE`.

versions_skip: No upstream release has the fix; only distro packages (Debian) do, listed under Are you affected.

changes.text: The stopgap now matches the researcher's wording: delete password-less rows, not lock them.
